clinicalPearls: Transient ultra-brief stabs of head pain lasting seconds, occurring spontaneously without an identifiable trigger
Pains are felt in the distribution of the first division of the trigeminal nerve in most cases but may move between areas
There are no accompanying cranial autonomic features, which helps distinguish it from the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias
Attacks may occur once or many times a day with an irregular pattern
It is more common in people who also have migraine
A subset responds to indometacin, though pains are often too brief to warrant treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Primary stabbing headache is an idiopathic disorder thought to arise from transient spontaneous discharges within trigeminal nociceptive pathways, without structural cause in the primary form. Its association with migraine and other primary headaches suggests shared central pain-modulating mechanisms. When stabs are consistently localised to one fixed site, an underlying structural lesion in that region should be considered.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary stabbing pain from a structural lesion
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on the characteristic brief stabs
Neurological examination to exclude focal signs
Neuroimaging if pains are strictly fixed in location or examination is abnormal
Review for coexisting migraine or other primary headache
redFlags: Stabs consistently confined to one fixed location
New onset in an older patient with other concerning features
Progressive change in pattern or associated deficits
reference.prognosis: The disorder is benign and often intermittent, with many patients needing no treatment and attacks tending to fluctuate over time.
pitfalls: Assuming a fixed-site stab is primary without imaging
Confusing it with trigeminal neuralgia, which has cutaneous triggers
Overtreating pains that are too brief to target
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Reassurance with no pharmacological treatment for most patients, since attacks are usually too brief to treat
Preventive indometacin for frequent or troublesome stabs, to which a subset responds well
Gastric protection with a proton pump inhibitor when indometacin is used
Alternative preventives such as gabapentin, melatonin or a cyclo-oxygenase-2 inhibitor when indometacin is ineffective or not tolerated
Identification and treatment of coexisting migraine or other primary headache
Neuroimaging and specialist referral if stabs are strictly fixed in one location or neurological examination is abnormal
